title: OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE
summary: A web app gets permission to read a user's calendar without ever seeing the user's password. Follow the browser redirects, the server-to-server token request, and what happens when a stolen code is replayed.

steps.label: GET /connect
steps.title: The user clicks "Connect calendar"
steps.desc: The user wants the client app to read their calendar. The app has no permission yet, so it starts an OAuth authorization request.

steps.label: make state + PKCE pair
steps.title: The client prepares two secrets for this attempt
steps.desc: The client generates a random state value and a random code_verifier, and keeps both in the user's session. It derives code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA-256(code_verifier)). Only the challenge will travel through the browser.

state.title: Client app: session for this browser
head: Key
Value

notes: state ties the answer to this browser session (protection against cross-site request forgery).
The verifier and challenge are PKCE (RFC 7636). They let the authorization server check later that whoever redeems the code is the same party that started the request.

steps.label: 302 to /authorize
steps.title: The client redirects the browser to the authorization server
steps.desc: The client answers with an HTTP redirect. The Location header points at the authorization endpoint and carries the request as query parameters.

rows: Asks for an authorization code, not a token.
Public identifier the client was given when it registered.
Random value the client will check when the browser comes back.
SHA-256 of the code_verifier, base64url encoded. The verifier itself stays on the client.

steps.label: GET /authorize?...
steps.title: The browser follows the redirect
steps.desc: The browser requests the authorization endpoint. This is the front channel: everything in the URL is visible to the browser, its history and anything else that can read the address.

rows: Asks for an authorization code, not a token.
Public identifier the client was given when it registered.
Random value the client will check when the browser comes back.
SHA-256 of the code_verifier, base64url encoded. The verifier itself stays on the client.

steps.label: known client + redirect?
steps.title: The authorization server checks the client and redirect URI
steps.desc: Before showing anything, the server looks up client_id and compares redirect_uri with the one registered for that client. Both match, so the request continues.
notes: If the redirect URI does not match, the server must not redirect the browser to it. It shows the user an error page instead, so a code can never be sent to an address an attacker supplied.

steps.label: login + consent page
steps.title: The server asks the user to sign in and approve
steps.desc: The authorization server shows its own sign-in page, then a consent screen: "Client app wants to read your calendar".
notes: How the user signs in (password, passkey, an existing session) is up to the authorization server. OAuth does not define it.

steps.label: sign in + approve
steps.title: The user signs in and approves the request
steps.desc: The user's credentials go to the authorization server only. The client app never sees them. This is the point of the whole flow.

steps.label: issue one-time code
steps.title: The server issues a short-lived authorization code
steps.desc: The server creates a code and records what it is bound to: the client, the redirect URI and the code_challenge from the request. The code is not a token. It is a one-time voucher for one.
notes: RFC 6749 recommends a lifetime of at most 10 minutes. Many servers use about a minute.

steps.label: 302 to /cb?code=...
steps.title: The server redirects back with the code
steps.desc: The browser is sent to the client's redirect URI. The code and the unchanged state value ride in the query string.

steps.label: GET /cb?code=...&state=...
steps.title: The browser delivers the code to the client
steps.desc: The code passes through the browser, so it may be seen there. That is acceptable only because a code alone is not enough to get a token.

steps.label: state matches session?
steps.title: The client checks state against the session
steps.desc: The state in the URL equals the state stored in this browser's session, so the response belongs to a request this user started here. A missing or different value means the client must stop.

state.title: Client app: session for this browser
head: Key
Value

steps.label: POST /token code + verifier
steps.title: The client exchanges the code for tokens
steps.desc: The client calls the token endpoint directly, server to server (the back channel). It authenticates with its own credentials and sends the code together with the code_verifier it kept secret.

rows: Must equal the one used in the authorization request.
Sent for the first time here. It never went through the browser.

steps.payload:
POST /token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com
Authorization: Basic czZCaGRSa3F0MzpnWDFmQmF0M2JW
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code
&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA
&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclient.example.com%2Fcb
&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
notes: The Authorization header is the client_id and client secret (HTTP Basic). An app that cannot keep a secret, such as a mobile or single-page app, sends client_id only and relies on PKCE.

steps.label: verify code + PKCE
steps.title: The server verifies everything the code was bound to
steps.desc: Every check must pass. The last one is PKCE: the server hashes the code_verifier it just received and compares the result with the code_challenge it stored. Then it marks the code as used.

state.title: Token request checks
head: Check
Result
rows: Code exists, not expired, not used
Code was issued to this client

steps.label: 200 access token
steps.title: The server returns an access token
steps.desc: The response is JSON and must not be cached. The access token is what the client will present to the API. The refresh token lets it get a new access token later without involving the user.
steps.payload:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-store

{
  "access_token": "2YotnFZFEjr1zCsicMWpAA",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "refresh_token": "tGzv3JOkF0XG5Qx2TlKWIA",
  "scope": "calendar.read"
}

steps.label: GET /events + Bearer token
steps.title: The client calls the API with the token
steps.desc: The access token goes in the Authorization header. "Bearer" means whoever holds the token can use it, which is why it is only ever sent over TLS and never through the browser's address bar.
steps.payload:
GET /events HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer 2YotnFZFEjr1zCsicMWpAA

steps.label: token valid for this?
steps.title: The resource server validates the token
steps.desc: The API checks that the token is genuine, has not expired and covers this request (scope calendar.read). It passes.
notes: OAuth 2.0 does not say how the API validates a token. Two common ways: the token is a signed JWT the API can verify itself (RFC 9068), or the API asks the authorization server (token introspection, RFC 7662).
A missing, expired or invalid token gets 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header. A valid token without the needed scope gets 403 insufficient_scope.

steps.label: 200 calendar events
steps.title: The API returns the user's calendar
steps.desc: The client has the data it asked for. At no point did it handle the user's password, and its access is limited to the scope the user approved.

steps.label: POST /token copied code
steps.title: What if: someone replays a copied code
steps.desc: Suppose an attacker copied the code from the redirect URL (from browser history, a log file or a malicious app on the device) and sends it to the token endpoint. They have the code, but not the code_verifier.

rows: The real one never left the client app.

steps.label: refuse: reused, no verifier
steps.title: The server refuses the code
steps.desc: Two independent checks fail. The code has already been used, and the verifier does not hash to the stored challenge. Either one is enough to refuse.
steps.fail: An authorization code works once, and only together with the code_verifier that matches its code_challenge. The attacker has neither a fresh code nor the verifier.

state.title: Token request checks
head: Check
Result
rows: Code exists, not expired, not used
Code was issued to this client

notes: When a code is presented a second time, the server should also revoke the tokens it issued from that code, because it cannot tell which caller was the genuine one.

steps.label: 400 invalid_grant
steps.title: The attacker gets an error, not a token
steps.desc: The token endpoint answers 400 Bad Request with the error code invalid_grant. No token is issued.

simplifications: TLS is assumed everywhere and not drawn. Every arrow here is an HTTPS request or response.
The login and consent exchange is two steps. Real sign-in is several requests and may include multi-factor authentication.
The client is a confidential web app with a client secret. Public clients (mobile and single-page apps) send no secret and depend on PKCE alone.
Refresh token use and rotation, token revocation and expiry handling are left out.
How the resource server validates the access token is summarised in one step; it differs between providers.
OpenID Connect (ID tokens, nonce, user info) is a layer on top of this flow and is not shown.
In the replay case the three failed checks are shown together; a real server stops at the first one that fails.
Token values are the short examples from the RFCs. Real tokens are longer.

sources.title: RFC 6749: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework, sections 4.1, 5.1, 5.2 and 10.12
